---
title: "Node Composition"
---

Composition lets you decide **at deploy time** — not compile time — whether the
pieces of your control stack run as separate processes or share a single one.
The same node binary can run standalone via `ros2 run` or be loaded into a
shared container alongside other nodes, with no change to the node code. This is
what makes a "composable control stack" possible: controller, estimator, and
allocator can be co-located for low latency in production, yet still launched
individually for debugging.

---

## Why it matters for a control stack

A control stack passes high-rate data along a chain: estimator -> controller ->
allocator, with odometry and setpoints flowing every loop iteration. When these
nodes live in separate processes, every message crosses a DDS boundary and is
serialized, copied, and deserialized.

Loading them into one **component container** enables intra-process
communication: messages are passed by shared pointer with no serialization. On
the hot path this removes a source of latency and jitter that directly affects
control quality.

::: {.callout-note}
Intra-process transport only kicks in when both endpoints are in the same
container *and* the node is built with `use_intra_process_comms`. QoS still has
to match — see [QoS Profiles](qos-profiles.qmd). PX4 `/fmu/*` topics cross the
DDS bridge regardless, so zero-copy only helps for traffic *between your own
nodes*.
:::

---

## Three ways to compose

| Style | How | When |
|-------|-----|------|
| Manual | A custom executable that instantiates several components by `#include` | Fixed, known-at-compile-time set of nodes |
| Runtime | Start a generic container, then `ros2 component load` nodes into it | Interactive bring-up, experimentation |
| Launch-time | `ComposableNodeContainer` describes the container and its nodes in a launch file | Production deployment |

Launch-time composition is what the bringup package uses. See the full
`ComposableNodeContainer` example in
[Bringup Package](../setup/ros2-bringup-package.qmd).

---

## Writing a node as a component

A node needs two things to be loadable into a container.

**1. A constructor that accepts `NodeOptions`** and forwards them to the base
`Node`:

```cpp
namespace my_pkg {

class Controller : public rclcpp::Node {
public:
    explicit Controller(const rclcpp::NodeOptions& options = rclcpp::NodeOptions())
    : Node("controller", options) {
        // ... subscriptions, publishers, timer ...
    }
};

}  // namespace my_pkg
```

The `options` argument is how the container injects parameters, remappings, and
intra-process settings at load time. A node that hardcodes `Node("controller")`
without forwarding options cannot be composed.

**2. Registration with the component factory:**

```cpp
#include "rclcpp_components/register_node_macro.hpp"
RCLCPP_COMPONENTS_REGISTER_NODE(my_pkg::Controller)
```

plus the matching `rclcpp_components_register_node` call in CMake. The full
package layout — `package.xml` depend, CMake target, and the standalone
`main.cpp` entry point — is on the
[C++ Node Package](../setup/ros2-cpp-package.qmd) page.

---

## Container variants

The container you launch picks the executor model for everything loaded into it:

| Container | Executor | Use for |
|-----------|----------|---------|
| `component_container` | One `SingleThreadedExecutor` shared by all components | Simple stacks; callbacks never run in parallel |
| `component_container_mt` | One `MultiThreadedExecutor` shared by all components | Parallel callbacks; pair with callback groups |
| `component_container_isolated` | One executor per component | Strong isolation between nodes |

For a real-time loop, `component_container_mt` plus callback groups is how you
keep a slow subscription from starving the control timer — the timer runs in a
`MutuallyExclusive` group on its own thread while other callbacks proceed
independently. See the callback-group discussion in
[Control Loop Architecture](control-loop.qmd).

---

## The constructor gotcha

::: {.callout-warning}
A component **must not block or do long-running work in its constructor**. The
container loads components synchronously: anything that blocks in the
constructor stalls the load (and any other node loaded after it). Do not wait
for the first odometry message, sleep, or spin in the constructor.
:::

Defer that work to a timer or a callback. A control node that needs an initial
state should arm a one-shot `create_wall_timer`, or simply guard its control
loop with a "have I received state yet?" check — the same state-validity guard
used in [Control Loop Architecture](control-loop.qmd) — rather than waiting in
the constructor.

---

## Verifying composition

List the containers and the components loaded in them:

```bash
# Show running containers
ros2 component list

# Example output:
# /my_container
#   1  /controller
#   2  /estimator
```

Load a component into a running container by hand (runtime composition):

```bash
ros2 component load /my_container my_pkg my_pkg::Controller
```

To confirm two nodes really share a process, check that they report the same
PID:

```bash
ros2 node info /controller   # then /estimator -- both map to one container PID
ps -ef | grep component_container
```

If the nodes show different PIDs, they did not compose — check that each node is
registered with `RCLCPP_COMPONENTS_REGISTER_NODE`, that the workspace is sourced
in the launching shell, and that the `plugin` name in the launch file matches
the registered class exactly.
